title: Joining Troy Floyd's band in Texas at 17
summary: Albert traces Floyd's band back to Alphonso Trent, tells how he left his three-piece band, and was hired on the spot without audition by Floyd.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Well, tell me a little bit more about Troy Floyd's band. I don't know too much about it, it's what you've told me.

Well, the history of Troy Floyd's band goes way back to the days of Alfonso Trent, who was a band that was organized with Texas musicians and Arkansas, because Trent originally was from a little town of Fort Smith, Arkansas. His estate was still there, I visited the estate just a couple of three years ago. And Trent was playing at the Adolphus Hotel, incidentally the first name of a band to be put into one of these big establishments. So Troy had his band organized with mostly Texas men. And the great trumpet player that was in his band, Ben O'Kennedy, quit Troy's band in Galveston. And I got worried about him leaving the band through Chester Clark, who was the trumpet player with Trent, wonderful trumpet player, tremendous. He said, you should wire Troy Floyd because he'll need a man in that seat and he'll fit it. I had my little three piece band and they joined another couple of musicians in Dallas. So I decided just to take a chance because my goal was set to become a great musician. And I tried and he asked me to wait for him that he would interview me when he got to Dallas. So I told the boys in the band that I thought I was going to quit them and I received them that they got back to New Orleans or do whatever they wanted to do. I could try to get them a job in another band if they wanted to stay around Texas. So they decided it would be better for them to come back to New Orleans. So Troy didn't listen to me play. He just put me in the automobiles and went out to East Texas to Eastland. And that was the first time that he heard me just tune my horn. He said, man, what a beautiful sound. How did I do it? And I said, well, I'm not. And incidentally, I was only 17 years old. So I got the job from just him and him. He blew my horn. And he was a man. He became the first chair man, also the feature man, because out of 10 musicians, I don't think there was about three or four of us that could be considered readers.
